newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ex-Frankfurt RFS prices fall as truck competition.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Frankfurt RFS prices fall as truck competition.

text.p: Prices for road transportation of air cargo from Frankfurt to domestic and European destinations are falling despite an increase in volumes, a Reuters' survey showed.

Demand from air cargo shippers and freight forwarders for road feeder services (RFS) is rising in line with market growth and as airlines use smaller aircraft in Europe and centralise cargo operations at hubs, industry sources said.
But de-regulation of the German road transport market, new suppliers entering the RFS market and increasing price competition are putting strong pressure on rates, they added.

Demand for tracking and tracing systems and electronic data interchange (EDI) of shipment information is becoming a more important factor in choice of supplier, according to both airline and trucking managers.
High handling charges at German airports are also prompting trucking companies to operate out of off-airport centres, particularly in Hamburg, Cologne, Duesseldorf and Hanover, they said.
Trucked air cargo refers to air freight shipments entered on airway bills and carried by truck from the airport of origin either to a destination airport or for onward transportation by air.

Official figures on the size of the German road feeder market do not exist but industry sources point to up to one million tonnes a year, or more than 30 percent of the total market, if estimates of off-airport tonnage, not recorded in airport statistics, are included.
The total value of the RFS market in Germany is hence at least 50 million marks given minimum rates of up to 50 marks per shipment, sources said.

At least 400,000 tonnes of trucked airfreight passes through Frankfurt airport, the main German air cargo gateway, each year in addition to the 1.37 million tonnes of flown freight, airport officials believe.
Purchasers of RFS services are mostly airlines, or forwarders, while some of the trucking companies also provide cargo handling services.
Prices for ad-hoc consignments are negotiatable and tend to be higher than the fixed rates agreed between airlines and truckers for long-term contracts, observers noted.
Lufthansa Cargo, by far the largest trucking client in Germany, said it has contracted 40 companies to operate scheduled services throughout Europe.
Hartmut Flessa, Lufthansa road and rail manager, said it was able to purchase space at highly attractive prices due to its volume of 350,000 tonnes a year.
Two-thirds of LCAG's trucking needs were covered by scheduled services with fixed departures and the rest was purchased on the spot market, he added.
Flessa said: "The cargo volumes are not developing so strongly this year. We estimate trucking growth of about three percent this year."
The airline had an average truck load factor of about 50 percent with an average of six tonnes per truck last year.
Flessa said the main Lufthansa routes within Germany were to Hamburg, Munich and Berlin.

In Europe, prices to Amsterdam tended to be lower than southbound to Frankfurt due to lower demand while there was very strong northbound demand from Milan to Frankfurt for Italian exports but more empty space on southbound trips.
Willem Heeren, managing director of large Dutch trucking company Jan de Rijk, said: "It is a constant trend of the last year or so that rates are falling. There are more players in the market."
"A lot of airlines go for the cheapest offers and do not always go for quality but we believe there is a place in the market for a high quality service as well as for low prices," he added.
Jan de Rijk operated RFS services across Europe for some 35 airline clients with 70 percent of truck departures as scheduled services and the remainder as ad-hoc trips, Heeren said.
The family-owned firm had shown growth of 15 percent in recent years and expected a total turnover of 100 million marks this year, he added.
Heeren said Jan de Rijk had invested one million guilders in its new RITTS tracking and tracking system which monitored trucks by satellite and gave airlines real-time online information.
"If an airline receives a message that a truck is going to arrive late (for a flight), then it can sell that space and not fly with a smaller load," he explained.
The RITTS system was a key reason why Jan de Rijk had secured an exclusive two million mark Germany trucking contract from British Airways last autumn, he added.

Winfried Meyer, BA trucking manager, said the airline was trying to concentrate business on only a few trucking companies such as Jan de Rijk to keep costs down and so that "we have only one partner, one invoice and one computer interface".
He confirmed that the Dutch trucker won the Germany distribution contract in particular due to its ability to offer specialised tracking and tracing through its RITTS system.
Meyer added that BA has also started a three times a week RFS service from Vienna via Linz to Munich to target the Austrian market with freight flown from Munich to the airline's London hubs.
Hermann Schleinbecker, Frankfurt manager of Convent GmbH Air Cargo Road Transport, one of the largest German trucking companies, said: "In 1997 I see only a small market growth and falling prices."
This matched the moderate growth in air cargo flown to and from Germany this year, he added.
Schlienbecker said Convent, with a share of 50 to 60 percent of the Frankfurt market for consolidated airfreight shipments, had Hamburg, Munich, Nuremberg, Bremen and Hanover as its strongest routes.
Leading airline clients included Delta Air Lines and American Airlines but forwarders were also important clients, he added.
Korean Air Lines said it was now offering airlines the chance to purchase spare KAL truck capacity under a new European road trucking system launched after a four-month test last autumn.

Martin Wildner, supervisor import cargo traffic, said the system allowed all seven KAL stations in Europe to dispatch loads directly on to trucks as though they were aircraft and reports truck arrivals back to each office.
KAL was responsible for contracting trucking partners while Frankfurt Airport airfreight department (FAG) did the documentation and handling.
"With this system we are improving our import service so that imports function like exports, and have increased speed and flexibility," Wildner said.
But Korean Air was also seeking to open up the system to other airlines who could purchase spare Korean truck capacity to different European destinations, he added.
"I invite other airlines to join our trucking system. If we have more partners and more volume, we and the other airlines can improve our services in Europe and Germany and decrease costs."
A spokesman for Rutges, the second large Dutch RFS specialist, said trucking prices were stable at present while volumes were rising leading to pressure on rates.
The company was also developing its own tracking and tracing system at present, he added.
At American Airlines, Christine Mohr, who is responsible for trucking and ground services, said that prices for full-load trucks appeared to be falling.
A particular problem for airlines were the high cargo handling fees of airports, she added.

A spokesman for Emery Airfreight said the falling RFS rates had been prompted by the de-regulation of the German truck transportation market over the last few years and the number of new entrants into the market.
Overall, RFS volumes appeared to be rising and would certainly increase more than prices, he added. - Reuters Air Cargo Newsroom Tel +44 171 542 7706 Fax 5017
